newsitem.title: USA: Russia's fiscal gap sparks worries in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Russia's fiscal gap sparks worries in U.S..

text.p: The green light to restart a stalled $10 billion International Monetary Fund lending programme to Russia serves more as a source of moral support than as a promise of effective financial aid to the Russian economy, according to U.S. specialists.

Increased borrowing by the Russian government, both in the Russian domestic treasury bill market and in the overseas Eurobond market, has dwarfed the IMF loan in attempting to plug the widening fiscal deficit. And U.S. investors increasingly are bracing for turbulence ahead.

IMF managing director Michel Camdessus said in Moscow recently he was ready to recommend the loan resumption to Russia. The disbursements for this year have been suspended because of concerns about the state's low rate of tax collection.

Gretchen Rodkey, an analyst at Bear, Stearns and Co., said Camdessus's vocal support gave weight in the new reformist cabinet lead by Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov, which amounted to an "advance vote of confidence."
While the stance required personal courage, Camdessus's gesture was in line with his previous position on helping Russian reforms, she said.
But the second tranche to be disbursed this year is likely to face much closer scrutiny and at least as many delays as in 1996, U.S. banking sources said.

Unlike the disbursement of the first tranche in 1996, when Russia was in constant turmoil because of a close presidential election and President Boris Yeltsin's long illness, this time there are few extenuating circumstances to postpone further badly needed reforms, said a senior analyst with a U.S. bank.
The pressure is on the new cabinet to boost tax collection, but stiff battles are expected with powerful industry groups that evade paying taxes.
The IMF has demanded that a tax code be submitted to the Duma (parliament) as a condition for disbursing the loans.

A tax code, even if passed in the Duma and enacted as law, would remain on paper, unless enforceable which is open to doubt under the current legal system, said Vladimir Kvint, director of emerging markets at Arthur Andersen.
The current chaos in tax collection is only one of the symptons of a deep economic crisis, which Kvint described as "the criminalization of the economy."

Ariel Cohen, senior economist at the Heritage Foundation, pointed out that Russia is a net exporter of capital -- some $20 billion fled the country last year, twice the amount of the IMF's three-year loan.
Unless Russia implements further economic restructuring in industry by breaking up monopolies and engaging in legal, agricultural, and military reforms, IMF aid is not justified, he said.
"It's like pouring water into a bucket with a huge hole in the bottom," Cohen said.

But better tax collection offers the only hope to stem the deterioration of Russia's fiscal conditions, said Jeffrey Anderson, director of the European department at the Institute of International Finance.

Russia's fiscal deficit last year totalled 9.6 percent of its Gross Domestic Product, he estimated. The 1997 budget set a fiscal deficit target of 7.5 percent of GDP based on a revenue projection which was widely seen as unrealistic.

"The Russian government has to build confidence in the economy and bring down the interest rates," Anderson said, noting that soaring interest expenses threaten to widen the fiscal gap, and stifle economic growth.
In a sustainable stabilisation programme, the real interest rate should not exceed the annual growth rate, he said.

The IMF projects the Russian economy could grow 6.0 percent by the turn of the century. It shrank 6.0 percent last year and many private economists expected it to turn a small rate of positive growth this year.

Foreign holdings of short-term debt are set to rise with the liberalisation of non-resident access to the Russian domestic treasury bill market, a move that was announnced earlier this month, market sources said.
The liberalisation, which had been widely anticipated, with most details known in advance, held no surprise for the market, they said.
